ABIG: Large US companies the manager sees as high-quality, enduring businesses, picked with conviction, with technology and internet giants the biggest names. It's a concentrated core growth holding: a few big positions lead, so it can pull ahead of the market or trail it by a wide margin.
AHYB: High-yield corporate bonds, the junk-rated debt companies issue, hand-picked by active managers across many industries in small slices. It's the income workhorse role with credit risk attached: interest payments are generous, and prices slide when investors worry about defaults or the economy.
AIVI: Value-priced companies in developed markets outside North America, chosen with the help of artificial intelligence models, led by banks at nearly two-fifths. The AI layer is the twist on plain value investing, tilting the portfolio as the models spot shifting patterns in prices and financials.
CLOC: Collateralized loan obligations, bundles of company loans repackaged into slices with different risk levels, actively picked across the quality spectrum. It pays higher interest than most bond funds; the trade-off is complexity and prices that can gap down when loan markets seize up.
DDFN: Large US stocks in a two-way design over each year starting in November: it can gain when the market rises, up to a cap, and can also gain when the market dips a little, with a buffer against bigger drops. The trade-off is smaller gains when the market runs strongly.
DIVL: Companies with long histories of paying dividends and the strength to keep raising them, spread across energy, banks, health care and industrials. It's a value-leaning income holding for the core of a portfolio, built for a payout that grows over time rather than the highest yield today.
DIVP: Dividend-paying value stocks across health care, banks, staples and energy, with covered calls sold on part of the portfolio to add extra income. It's an income-first stock holding in the Cullen value tradition: steadier and higher-paying than the broad market, with less growth punch.
DYFI: A dynamic mix of bond funds spanning mortgage bonds, high-yield debt, loan bundles and inflation-protected bonds, rotated by an active manager toward whichever corner looks best. It's a one-stop bond portfolio with leverage in the mix, so it can out-earn plain bond funds and fall harder when credit markets crack.
EFAD: Companies in developed markets outside North America that have raised their dividends for at least ten straight years, spread across health care, industrials, technology and banks. It's an income-and-quality overseas core holding; the long growth streak requirement tilts it toward steadier firms than a plain foreign fund.
EFAS: Fifty of the highest dividend-paying companies in Europe, Australasia and the Far East, weighted equally, led by banks, insurers and utilities. It's a maximum-income overseas holding: the payouts are the point, and equal weighting plus a high-yield screen make it jumpier and more bank-heavy than broad foreign funds.
EMCR: Emerging market companies that either meet climate criteria or have committed to cutting their greenhouse gas emissions, led by Asian chip makers. It's the climate-screened version of an emerging markets core holding, though technology giants still dominate, so it behaves much like a standard emerging fund.
EMM: Emerging market companies with China left out entirely, led by Taiwanese and Korean chip makers, with big slices in India and Brazil through sister funds. It's a focused answer to China risk in emerging markets, though the result is heavily a technology and Asia fund in practice.
EZET: A fund that holds ether itself, the cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network, so its price follows the coin held in custody. It offers stock-market access to the second-biggest cryptocurrency without a crypto account, and it will swing just as hard as ether does, which is to say a lot.
FHYS: High-yield bonds with short times left to maturity, the junk-rated debt of companies, chosen to pay high interest while limiting how long each loan is exposed. Short maturities make it calmer than most junk bond funds, but the credit risk of weaker borrowers remains fully in place.
GCLO: Investment-grade slices of collateralized loan obligations, the higher-rated layers of bundles of company loans, which get paid before riskier layers. It pays more than Treasury bonds while staying in high credit quality territory, though CLO structures are complex and can cheapen quickly in panics.
GEEQ: US stocks combined with options strategies that trade some upside for a higher stream of income, actively managed across companies and other funds. It's an income-first equity holding: payouts come before growth, so it will trail the market in strong rallies and cushion only part of any decline.
GRW: Growth companies the manager believes will endure through industry change, spread between technology and aerospace and industrial firms. 'Durable' is the filter: it favors businesses with lasting advantages over flashy stories, so it aims for growth with a steadier temperament than most growth funds.
GURU: The favorite US stocks of a select group of hedge funds, copied from their public disclosure filings and weighted roughly equally. Health care and technology lead right now; the filings arrive with a lag, so the fund holds what the gurus owned last quarter, not necessarily what they own today.
HERO: Video game companies from around the world: game publishers, streaming and esports platforms, and the hardware and software firms behind them. It's a focused bet on gaming as entertainment, driven by hit titles and console cycles, so it can be feast or famine as big releases land or flop.
HYDW: US high-yield corporate bonds chosen from the calmer end of the junk bond market, the issuers whose prices historically move less with the broader high-yield pack. It's an income holding that tries to keep junk bond payouts while trimming the drama, though it still falls in real credit panics.
IBIJ: Inflation-protected US Treasury bonds all maturing in 2033, in a fund that wraps up in October of that year. The principal grows with inflation, protecting purchasing power to a fixed end date, though the price still rises and falls with interest rates before then.
IRTR: A retirement fund for people already at or near retirement, holding about three-fifths bonds and two-fifths stocks in a mix that stays conservative. It keeps adjusting slowly toward safety over time, offering a single-holding landing spot for money being drawn down in retirement.
JANT: Large US stocks paired with options that absorb roughly the first tenth of any loss over each year starting in January, in exchange for a cap on gains. The smaller buffer means a higher cap than stronger-shield funds, and part of the protection may be used up if you buy mid-year.
JELM: Equity-linked securities, investments that pay regular income while their returns stay tied to stock markets, in a moderate-risk design. It's an income holding built from structured products rather than plain stocks and bonds, so the payouts are steadier than dividends but gains are limited by design.
KOOL: A rotation portfolio moving between US stock sectors, individual market leaders and some overseas stocks, currently spread across health care, energy and technology. It aims to stay in whichever part of the market is working; frequent rotation means it can also be wrong-footed when leadership flips quickly.
LENS: A thematic fund that bets on one big market story at a time; right now that means energy and mining companies plus gold and silver funds, a hard-assets portfolio. The theme can change as the manager's view shifts, so today's inflation hedge may become something else entirely.
MSOL: A trust holding Solana, a fast, low-fee blockchain network's token, and staking part of it to earn extra rewards. It gives stock-market access to a major but still speculative cryptocurrency, and like all single-coin trusts it will swing violently with that one token's price.
OVT: Short-term investment-grade corporate bonds held through a bond fund, with an options overlay that sells put options to add income on top. The overlay lifts the payout in calm times; if bond markets or stocks drop sharply, the sold puts can add losses a plain short-term bond fund would avoid.
PHDG: America's largest stocks paired with a volatility hedge: futures tied to the market's fear gauge, added in amounts that grow when markets get shaky. The hedge is meant to cushion crashes, and it costs performance in calm markets, so it trails plain stock funds most of the time.
PIPE: Master limited partnerships and energy infrastructure companies, the pipeline and storage firms paid to move oil and gas across North America. It's an income play run by a specialist manager; the payouts are generous, and the fund moves with energy markets and pipeline volumes rather than oil prices alone.
PJIO: A focused portfolio of growth companies outside the US, heavy on Asian chip makers and European industrial and aerospace firms. Jennison's growth style means a short list of companies expected to grow for years; it will look and behave very differently from a broad foreign market fund.
PRNT: The 3D printing ecosystem: printer makers, design software firms, scanning and measurement companies, and medical users of printed parts. It's a narrow ARK theme fund on a technology still finding its market, so it has swung widely as enthusiasm for additive manufacturing rose and faded.
PSCW: Large US stocks with a conservative structured outcome over each year starting in April, using layered options to cushion losses more than to chase gains. It's among the more defensive buffer-style funds: expect smaller drops in sell-offs and smaller gains in rallies than the market.
PSFD: Large US stocks with a flexible structured outcome over each year starting in January, using layered options to cushion the first part of losses while keeping a share of gains. The flex design adjusts the trade-off between protection and upside, so outcomes vary more than with fixed buffer funds.
QBSF: Large US stocks paired with options that absorb the first part of a drop over each outcome period, while gains above a set level stay uncapped rather than cut off. Allianz's buffer design is the draw; like all buffer funds, the protection in place shrinks if you buy after a fall.
QCJA: The Nasdaq's big growth companies with a conservative buffer over each year starting in January, absorbing a larger part of any loss than standard buffer funds in exchange for a lower cap on gains. Technology is about three-fifths, and the bigger cushion is the point for cautious growth investors.
QEMM: Emerging market companies blending three stock-picking styles at once: value, quality and low volatility, spread across Asia, Latin America and elsewhere. The three-factor mix is the point, aiming for a smoother emerging markets ride, though chip giants still dominate the top of the fund.
RAUS: US companies weighted by their fundamental size, things like sales, cash flow and dividends, rather than by stock market value. The fundamental weighting quietly trims whatever has run up and adds to what has lagged, giving it a value tilt compared with plain cap-weighted market funds.
RTRE: A go-anywhere bond portfolio mixing Treasuries, mortgage bonds, corporate debt, municipal bonds and foreign bonds, managed for total return rather than just income. The flexibility is the point: it can lean into whichever bond market looks best, which also means its risk profile shifts over time.
SGRT: Thirty large US companies chosen for the strength and growth of their earnings, dominated by data center and technology hardware firms at about three-fifths. It's a concentrated growth fund riding the computing build-out, so it swings more than broader growth funds and leans on a short list of winners.
SXQG: Large US companies chosen for quality growth: strong balance sheets and durable earnings, led by technology at about half the fund. It's an actively managed core growth holding aiming for a smoother ride than aggressive growth funds, favoring proven compounders over speculative stories.
TAFL: Long-term municipal bonds from across the US, managed with taxes actively in mind, mostly paying interest exempt from federal income tax. The long maturities mean bigger price swings when rates move, and the tax-aware approach can occasionally favor a taxable bond when the after-tax math works better.
TEKY: Next-generation technology companies worldwide: chip makers, computing hardware and the suppliers behind artificial intelligence, picked by active managers. It's a global growth bet beyond the usual US giants, heavy on Asian semiconductor names, so it swings with the chip cycle as much as with software trends.
THTA: Treasury bills with about a year of maturity, plus a credit spread options strategy layered on top to add extra yield beyond what the bills pay. It's a cash-like holding with a kick: the options introduce credit risk the bills alone would never have, so it is not risk-free.
TRND: A fund of five trend-following funds covering US large and mid-sized stocks, overseas stocks and US bonds, each able to shift to Treasury bills when its market trends down. The trend rules are the point: it's built to sidestep long declines, accepting missed rebounds when trends flip quickly.
TYLD: A tactical bond fund that rotates among bond types, Treasuries, corporate and high-yield among them, following a model toward the best yield for the risk. Right now it sits mostly in Treasury bills, which shows the defensive side: it will hide in cash-like safety when the model dislikes bonds.
VBCD: Corporate bonds that all mature around 2030, from phone companies, banks and other large firms, in a fund that wraps up at the end of that year. It works like one big bond with a known finish line, useful for money earmarked for a goal around 2030.
WCAP: Companies of any size chosen freely by an active manager, mostly large US growth names, with a few other funds mixed in for smaller and overseas exposure. Unconstrained means no index to answer to: the portfolio reflects the manager's best ideas, for better or worse.
WSGE: Stocks from around the world held through other funds, blending US and overseas markets with tilts toward quality and other proven stock traits. It's a one-stop global core holding from a wealth manager; the fund-of-funds build means the mix reflects their house view and can shift over time.
YBIT: An income strategy on bitcoin, using options on bitcoin funds to mimic owning the coin while selling calls for regular cash payouts. The payouts are the draw; the calls cap bitcoin's big rallies, and the fund still falls hard when bitcoin crashes, just with some premium income to soften it.
